items.question: Why do you think OpenAI’s early attempt to build a general-purpose visual web agent failed?
items.object: OpenAI’s early web-agent project
items.answer: If you look at OpenAI’s history, which is quite interesting, you’ll find that the first project it worked on after it was founded was exactly this: web agents—having a general-purpose visual agent click around on web pages. If you trace back to 2016, OpenAI’s first big project was this thing. Of course, their approach failed. I often tell this story to students in my deep-learning course: why did it fail? They only had reinforcement learning; they had no foundation model; they didn’t even have people collecting and labeling data. At the time they did not even have transformers. They used a large LSTM called ComNet to click around on web pages using reinforcement learning. It failed, and they laid off a lot of people.

items.object: OpenAI Operator’s release as a step toward general-purpose AI
items.answer: I think it represents a move toward generality. Models like o1 and o3 can think more deeply about focused problems, but there is no environmental interaction in the middle. That is the first point: no environmental interaction. Second, they are not multimodal. If you need a general-purpose brain, it needs not only deep thinking but also multimodality and the ability to form a closed-loop control system through environmental interaction. What is a closed loop? With o1, after you give it an instruction, there is no external interaction in the middle. It thinks for twenty seconds and gives you an answer; there is no feedback control in between. But the real world is different, right? If I want to operate software, or do an operation like Operator, I need to think for a while, click something, and look at the external feedback.

items.question: How do you understand the significance of OpenAI Operator’s ability to interact continuously with its environment?
items.object: OpenAI Operator’s capacity for continuous interaction
items.answer: Previously, things like 4o—whether image understanding or language-instruction understanding—were all single-step, or their actions were one step. You rarely had a model that could truly say: I see an observation, take one action, see a new observation, then take the next action. The capability to continuously conduct many rounds of interaction did not exist before. Of course, I knew this would happen, because it is a horizontal capability that a general-purpose agent must have. The vertical axis is depth of thought; the horizontal axis is breadth, your general capability. It must have this capability, and OpenAI has finally brought it out.

items.question: How do you understand OpenAI Operator’s relationship to o1 and o3?
items.object: OpenAI Operator’s relationship to o1 and o3
items.answer: I think it is more that it follows the post-training reinforcement-learning path, but it has not gone as far to the extreme as o1 and o3. It has moved sideways in breadth—outward, broader. Very simply, if you observe Operator’s chain of thought, it is relatively short. If you look at the chains of thought released for o1 and o3, they are very long and contain a lot of backtracking. But Operator’s chain of thought is relatively short; its backtracking mainly occurs in its actions. For example, you may see an agent click a web page and discover that it has been clicking for a long time without opening it, right? It will go back. Its backtracking happens in action, not in its chain of thought. So I tend to think it is probably not a model as extreme as o3. It may be more like o1, but a multimodal closed-loop o1—an agent-o1 version. That is my understanding. So I think it still has room: what if it had a better chain of thought? What if it had a better multimodal understanding model? What if it had better generalization? There is room. It is more like o1 in the multimodal world, or perhaps a position somewhat pre-o1.

items.question: Why do you think OpenAI gave Operator a separate entry point as a standalone product?
items.object: OpenAI’s decision to offer Operator as a standalone product
items.answer: My understanding is that this should be a different foundation model. I think it was made separate for two reasons. On one hand, it is clearly a foundation model different from o3. It is itself a model whose agent potential was elicited with multimodal data different from o3’s, and then trained with reinforcement learning, so its model characteristics must differ from o3’s, and relatively from o1 and o3 as well. From the product perspective, first, the model is different, so they put two models into it. Second, once you have two strong models, can you combine them? I actually think you can; you definitely can. So, in a sense, OpenAI also deliberately put this separate, more transitional intermediate-state model into a standalone product, and I think that is meaningful and makes sense. People are accustomed to using ChatGPT, and giving them such a completely different mode of use may indeed be better as a separate product.

items.question: What do you see as the essential technical ingredients for building an agent like OpenAI Operator?
items.object: The technical ingredients needed to build an agent like OpenAI Operator
items.answer:
I would still point to three things, the same as o1. First, you need a very good foundation model: a particularly good native multimodal foundation model. This is very important. In many of our own training experiences, in the report DeepSeek released previously, and in many models OpenAI itself has released, the foundation model is extremely important. So first, the multimodal foundation model must be good.

Second, you very clearly need high-quality data and tasks—a dataset. Very simply, go back to the examples Operator released. You see agents really close ads; they really say, I entered a web page and did not successfully click it, so I go back. These are very human-like actions. I believe OpenAI must have a considerable amount of this kind of data, because you still need it: its behavioral patterns are very different from those of the foundation model. So it must have prepared data for this. But my sense is that the volume need not be so large; compared with pre-training, post-training does not require as much data. Still, the data itself and the tasks must be well prepared. That is the second point: data.

The third is reinforcement learning. Besides a very good training system, reinforcement learning needs to be scaled up. In an agent environment, a troublesome part is that you also need an interactive environment afterward. Whether it is a web page or an operating system, this requires a lot of engineering optimization. It takes a great deal of effort, especially for large-scale training that may require thousands or ten thousand GPUs: how do you carry out those interactions efficiently? This is harder because with o1 or o3 solving math problems, there is no interaction in the middle; you simply let the model emit tokens. It is simple. But now, after emitting several hundred tokens, it has to click the screen. You need a computer waiting for the AI to click and simulating it, right? After the simulation, you let the AI emit more. The training system becomes more complex. Making it efficient and supporting efficient training is also a research problem.

So: a good base model, high-quality human data, and an efficient, large-scale agent-supporting reinforcement-learning system. Together, those three things produce a model like Operator.

items.question: How do you understand the Computer-Using Agent concept behind OpenAI’s Operator?
items.object: Computer-Using Agents (CUA) and their relationship to traditional language models and workflow agents
items.answer: I think the concept was actually first brought out by Claude. Anthropic introduced this concept relatively early in a newer model. The core difference is interaction capability. Traditional large models output tokens; they do not truly interact, receive new feedback, and then output again, right? Under this new concept, you want the model to be a closed-loop control system. Traditional large models are open-loop systems: after you give one instruction, the model outputs directly, without any feedback from anyone in the middle. But in this agent mode, it is a closed-loop system. After I receive an instruction, I output some tokens and proactively invoke something; at that point, my model expects that there will be subsequent feedback. The model then uses those new feedback signals to think through the next step. Thus, in training or in its context, it is not a fixed context—the context keeps changing. At the same time, it is multimodal. Those two things together make this new concept. In essence, though, the concept is not new. It was already the basic framework when the agent concept was introduced. Before Claude and OpenAI’s Operator, agents used agent frameworks, prompting, and engineering implementations to make an originally open-loop foundation model that was not specially trained for this task appear able to do it. But a new generation, such as Claude’s earlier Sonnet or Operator, is trained specifically for this task, so it performs much better and is much more intelligent than those traditional workflow agents.

items.question: How do you assess the challenge for Chinese teams trying to replicate OpenAI Operator?

Chinese teams previously could also use an open-source multimodal model and do some SFT, fine-tuning, or prompting to get somewhat similar effects, but there is a fairly big quality gap with models released by OpenAI or earlier by Anthropic. items.question: Why do you agree that 2025 is the year of agents?
items.object: 2025 as the year of agents
items.answer: I strongly agree. The reason is that the technology has arrived from all directions. For agents, if you want to make a truly general agent using reinforcement learning and this good training approach, what do you need? You really need a good foundation model. Data is actually OK, because many people know how to make data. So, putting the data itself aside, you need a good foundation model and a good, mature reinforcement-learning training framework. And now, starting with GPT-4o and GPT-4V, we can see foundation models getting better and better, reaching a state where their potential can increasingly be elicited. Then in 2024, you saw o1 and o3; domestic teams also began catching up in reinforcement learning. Many people now have reinforcement-learning technology, or at least have seen that o1 and o3 showed how much potential reinforcement learning plus a good foundation model can unlock. Naturally they will ask: what potential would a multimodal model plus reinforcement learning have? That is natural, right? We had pure text models, and with reinforcement learning we saw o1 and o3. The natural next thought is: what about multimodal models? And the most direct user-facing way to use multimodal models is this kind of agent, or an agent for general-purpose interfaces. So the technology has arrived, unimodality exists, and moving to multimodality is a natural evolution.

items.question: Why do you distinguish the data flywheel in AI from the data flywheel in recommendation systems?
items.object: The data flywheel in AI versus recommendation systems
items.answer: So, in the AI era, people always talk about the data flywheel, the data flywheel. But the data flywheel in the AI era is somewhat different. Data is a moat, but is it a flywheel? I do not think it is quite the same. I once worked on recommendation systems. In recommendation systems, you really have a data flywheel. What is a data flywheel? The system runs there; you do not manage it, just let it run, without major adjustments, and it should get better and better. For example, the more I click, whether I shop on Taobao or scroll videos on Douyin, the better it gets. The system’s team may not have done anything. But AI is not like that. AI may have a moat, lots and lots of data, but most of that data may be noise. You need very smart researchers and teams to spend a lot of time identifying the truly useful parts. So it is not an automatic flywheel. Even product feedback does not automatically start spinning; people still need to continually intervene to clean the data. It is really different from recommendation.

items.question: How do you understand the term “agent” that has become so widely discussed in the era of large language models?
items.object: The concept of an AI agent
items.answer: Yes, it is over-discussed. I have given talks about this before. I say that agent, in the earliest days, was a concept used in many places once AI was proposed. Agent originally comes from game theory, basically. We talk about two players or two agents playing rock-paper-scissors. We say two agents are playing a zero-sum game, right? It was a commonly used term first introduced in game theory, in game-like settings. Then in reinforcement learning, because it extends from game theory to sequential decision problems, we call an AI that interacts with an environment an agent—an intelligent agent interacting in an environment. So it was a relatively niche concept in game theory and reinforcement learning. Then, after large models arrived, suddenly everyone began talking about agents. In the era of large models, talking about agents often means that a large model can call interfaces in the external world.
